Railway ticket crisis: A question of public service, accountability and governance
item.description:
A basic question about public service arises from the apparent unavailability of train tickets from Dhaka to Sylhet for Friday, November 6.
Upaban Express (739) Dhaka departure 10pm, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 5am, 7 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for S_Chair, AC_B and Snigdha.
Jayentika Express (717) Dhaka departure 11:15 am, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 7pm, 6 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for AC_S, S_Chair and Snigdha.
Parabat Express (709) Dhaka departure 6:30am, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 1pm, 6 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for Snigdha, S_Chair and F_Seat.
Screenshots of the railway ticket-search page, captured on November 5, show zero available tickets in every class displayed for three services: Parabat Express, Jayentika Express, and Upaban Express. The situation is surprising enough to warrant a clear explanation from Bangladesh Railway.
Despite different departure times, the screenshots show zero available tickets in all the listed categories.
This raises an important question: Is the demand for travel to Sylhet on an ordinary Friday so exceptionally high that every listed seat on all three trains has been sold, or are there other factors affecting ticket availability?
The screenshots alone cannot establish whether all seats have genuinely been sold. Nor do they reveal how many passengers will actually board, how many tickets were allocated to different channels or quotas, or whether any technical or operational issue affected the online display. Those are precisely the questions that a transparent investigation should answer.
Bangladesh Railway should therefore verify the position on the ground. The Railway Secretary could form several effective inspection teams to examine the three Dhaka-Sylhet services.
The teams should compare the number of tickets issued with the number of passengers who actually board, check coach-wise occupancy, review quota and release arrangements, and examine whether tickets are being diverted, withheld or resold unlawfully.
The findings should be documented and made public, while protecting passengers’ personal information. If the investigation identifies irregularities or negligence, those responsible should face appropriate action under the applicable rules.
The issue also invites a wider reflection on the structure and performance of public institutions. Over time, railway administration has been given a dedicated department and then a separate ministry, with the associated senior administrative positions and public expenditure.
Institutional restructuring, however, should be judged by whether it improves the quality, reliability and accessibility of services -- not simply by the number of offices or senior posts created. The public is entitled to ask what measurable improvements have resulted from these changes.
The contrast with private transport is also worth examining. A passenger who approaches a private bus operator may sometimes find a seat for the following day, although the fare may be higher than the railway fare. This is not proof that private operators are always more efficient, or that railways can be assessed by exactly the same standards.
It does, however, highlight the importance of responsiveness, transparent booking, and reliable information. A public service should not leave passengers uncertain about whether tickets are genuinely sold out or simply unavailable through the channel they are using.
The answer is not necessarily to centralize every operational decision. Rather, Bangladesh needs clear central oversight, enforceable service standards, transparent ticket-allocation rules, reliable digital systems, and strong field-level monitoring.
Decentralized units must also be held to measurable performance targets. Where decentralization has weakened oversight or encouraged arbitrary practices, the arrangements should be reviewed and corrected.
Any reform -- centralized or decentralized -- must be based on evidence and must demonstrably improve public service.
There is also a public-finance dimension. When institutions fail to deliver the services expected of them, the state may face additional administrative costs, repeated interventions and avoidable losses.
Ultimately, public expenditure is funded by citizens, including through taxes. Preventing waste and ensuring that public officials perform their responsibilities are therefore not merely administrative concerns; they are matters of fairness to taxpayers.
The immediate request is straightforward: Let the Railway Secretary arrange an independent, practical check of the Dhaka-Sylhet trains and publish the findings.
Bangladesh Railway should explain how many tickets were released and sold, how many passengers travelled, whether all displayed seats were occupied, and whether any irregularity was found.
If the screenshots reflect genuine full occupancy, the public deserves accurate information about demand and capacity. If they do not, the reasons must be identified and corrected.
Citizens do not ask for institutions merely to exist; they expect them to serve. Public confidence in Bangladesh Railway will grow when ticketing is transparent, services are reliable, and responsibility is visible.
The real measure of governance is not the size of the administrative structure, but the quality of service experienced by ordinary people.
Md Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is a retired Additional Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration, Bangladesh.

item.title: Iranians burn giant poster of Trump and Netanyahu, demand revenge
item.description:
Following the drubbing of US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections, Iranians set fire to a giant poster featuring the American leader and his allies at a rally in Tehran.
In the capital’s central Enghelab square, crowds gathered to observe the burning of the poster which also featured his Vice President JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The war was started by Trump and Netanyahu, who launched a massive wave of surprise attacks against Iran which killed supreme leader Ayatollah Khamenei and others on February 28 and sparked the wider Middle East war.
The cheering audience waved red flags to demand revenge for Khamenei’s death.
“We will kill Trump,” read the slogan on some of the flags waved by the crowd as a song named “We Must Rise” mourning Khamenei blared from nearby speakers.
Earlier, thousands of Iranians had mocked Trump at an annual rally commemorating the US embassy takeover and hostage crisis that followed the 1979 Islamic revolution.
Wednesday’s public displays took place following the Republicans’ crushing losses in the midterm elections in which the Democrats seized control of Congress.
Trump admitted that the war he launched with Israel against Iran in February was a key factor in the electoral defeat.
Iranian officials have since taunted the US president, with security chief Mohsen Rezaei saying it marked a “political defeat” after Tehran “handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz” strait.

item.title: Samanta Shermeen resigns from NCP
item.description:
Samanta Shermeen has resigned from the National Citizen Party (NCP), saying the party has moved away from its founding values and failed to pursue the political reforms it had promised.
She announced her resignation in a Facebook post on Thursday, saying she had spent nearly a year trying to change the party’s direction from within.
“I had taken a different position on the question of the NCP forming an alliance about a year ago. I said Jamaat-e-Islami was not a suitable ally, either ideologically or strategically, and that the NCP would have to pay a heavy price for forming an alliance with the party,” she wrote.
Shermeen was named only a joint convener in the NCP’s new committee announced on October 23, a change that prompted discussion on social media about her apparent demotion.
In her post, she said that over the past 11 months she had submitted written complaints and proposals and taken part in discussions and debates at different levels of the party, based on her political understanding of its past actions and future direction.
She said she had considered it her political responsibility to try to prevent the party from taking the wrong course. She chose to pursue an ideological struggle within the organisation because challenging its policies through recognised forums was the only democratic way to bring about change.
“Today, I am bringing this nearly year-long struggle to an end because I no longer believe the NCP can remain sincere to the values on which it was founded,” she wrote.
Shermeen said she could have waited for a more opportune moment to resign, when her decision might have been linked to a specific party decision or action. But she considered such a wait pointless.
Even if the NCP eventually withdrew from an alliance with Jamaat, she said, she did not believe it could develop an independent identity, political outlook and programme outside the traditional political model.
She argued that political parties operating within the old system would obstruct, rather than facilitate, efforts to establish a new state order.
In her post, Shermeen outlined four major areas of disagreement with the party: its position on Jamaat and reform, its election strategy, women's political participation and its internal restructuring without a council.
Shermeen said the NCP had emerged with a commitment to reform and needed to ensure that existing power structures did not obstruct the transition to a democratic state.
She identified three areas requiring reform: constitutional changes to remove authoritarian and fascist foundations; legal reforms to make laws serve public welfare; and reforms to political parties and their structures to move away from colonial-era political practices.
She alleged that Jamaat-e-Islami did not consider any of these reforms part of its own political agenda and did not genuinely embrace reformist politics.
According to Shermeen, the party's ideological foundations and proposed state model were incompatible with democracy. She claimed Jamaat's support for reform was largely a way to appropriate the aspirations of the 2024 uprising.
She further alleged that Jamaat used democratic institutions and freedoms to pursue a political project that was contrary to democratic governance. She also criticised the party for not acknowledging its role in 1971 as a crime or apologising to the nation.
Shermeen said the NCP's decision to view Jamaat as an ally in the reform process had alienated ordinary Bangladeshis who supported liberal and democratic values.
She argued that the NCP's unclear political position had allowed Jamaat to overshadow its own identity, pushing it into reactive and supportive roles on various issues.
Shermeen said the 2026 election had the potential to become a political election that could bring structural change, rather than merely a transfer of power between parties.
She cited the elections of 1946, 1954, 1970 and 1990 as examples of polls that had brought broader political changes.
She argued that established political parties had sought to strip the 2026 election of the political character of the uprising and turn it into a conventional contest for power.
According to her, the NCP could have joined forces with those seeking to challenge the old political order or contested independently, even after the failures of the Consensus Commission, Election Commission and interim government's reform initiatives.
She claimed the party could have achieved a stronger result by pursuing that course, rather than joining an alliance led by a larger political party.
Shermeen said she had proposed five alternative ways for the NCP to increase its political influence without joining an electoral alliance such as the 11-party unity. However, the leadership did not follow those proposals.
She argued that prioritising electoral victory over broader political gains had also weakened the party's credibility in questioning election results under an unreformed system.
Referring to the death of Shaheed Osman Hadi, she said his candidacy in a challenging Dhaka constituency had been used as a justification for joining an alliance with a larger party, which she described as unreasonable and politically motivated.
Shermeen said women had played a decisive role in the 2024 mass uprising, serving as frontline protesters, protectors and catalysts for the movement.
Their participation, she wrote, was driven by political aspirations and demands for a fair share of power, equality and an end to oppression.
She accused conservative political groups of trying to push women out of the political space after the uprising, using social restrictions that had failed to prevent their participation during the movement.
Shermeen said the NCP had an opportunity to establish a different political culture based on gender equality, but had failed to ensure women's meaningful representation in leadership, decision-making and organisational power.
She alleged that the party had aligned itself with conservative, anti-women political tendencies and had marginalised women's voices in its decision-making process.
Women account for around 51% of Bangladesh's population, she noted, arguing that ignoring their voices meant excluding the political aspirations and experiences of more than half the population.
She said achieving equality in a society such as Bangladesh required more than equal opportunities. Women needed greater representation, authority and meaningful participation in decision-making to overcome entrenched power structures.
Shermeen also questioned whether women had been encouraged to stand at the forefront of the uprising because their leadership was recognised or because their presence was used as a protective shield in moments of danger.
If their courage and sacrifices were accepted during the movement but their political rights and share of power were denied after victory, she asked, what did recognition of their participation mean?
Shermeen said people had expected the NCP to establish a political structure different from those of traditional parties, with transparency in its finances and democratic practices within the organisation.
She criticised the party for restructuring its convening committee without holding a council, saying the move undermined internal democracy.
She argued that timely councils were essential for ensuring leadership legitimacy, accountability and representation. Without them, decision-making risked becoming concentrated in the hands of a small group.
According to Shermeen, the NCP had adopted the same practices it had criticised in older political parties, including suppressing dissent and limiting internal debate.
She said the restructuring had raised questions about the party's commitment to internal democracy and could undermine its credibility when demanding a fair and neutral electoral system at the national level.
After repeatedly urging the party to reconsider its positions on these issues, Shermeen said she had decided to resign because the leadership showed no willingness to change course.
In the final section of her statement, Shermeen called for a political movement based on national unity rather than division.
She said post-uprising Bangladesh needed a shared political vision that could bring people together despite differences in opinion, belief and identity.
The NCP, she said, had the opportunity to build such a political force under young leadership, but narrow political calculations had gradually weakened that possibility.
However, she added, the failure of one party or a group of leaders did not mean the end of the political aspirations that had brought people together.
Shermeen said a new political force should place Bangladesh's interests and the welfare of its people at the centre of its policies, rather than serving narrow interests or aligning itself with foreign powers.
She argued that the country's foreign policy should be guided by sovereignty and national interests, applying the same standards to agreements with India, the United States, China and other countries.
She also called for women's independent political participation, leadership and decision-making authority to be integral to the political structure.
Other priorities, she said, should include protecting and developing national capital, expanding domestic production and employment, reducing economic inequality and ensuring that public resources and policymaking serve the people.
Shermeen said young people now faced the challenge of building a political alliance that could accommodate differences without allowing division to dominate politics.
“I am committed to working as part of this effort,” she wrote, inviting those interested in discussing the ideas to contact her and join the effort to build a democratic Bangladesh.

AIUB participates in QS Higher Ed Summit in Indonesia
item.description:
American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) participated in the QS Higher Ed Summit: Asia Pacific 2026, held from November 3-5 at the Bali International Convention Centre in Indonesia.

The AIUB delegation included Founder Member and Vice Chairman Ishtiaque Abedin, Board of Trustees member Dr Carmen Z Lamagna, Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Saiful Islam, Senior Assistant Professor Carlin Noelle Zita Lamagna, Director of Ranking and Global Engagement Mashiour Rahman, and Head of Public Relations Md Abu Mia Akhanda.
Participating as part of the Bangladesh Pavilion, AIUB joined other Bangladeshi institutions in presenting the country's higher education sector to international delegates.
During the summit, the delegation met with QS officials to discuss preparations for an upcoming QS event in Bangladesh, which AIUB is scheduled to host.
The delegation also held discussions with representatives of universities and educational organizations on potential academic partnerships, research collaboration, and faculty and student exchange programs.

Study: Locally made aluminium pots can leach lead into food
item.description:
Locally manufactured aluminium cooking pots can release lead into food, exposing families to the toxic metal through everyday meals, according to a study by the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) and Stanford University. Lead release was highest during the first uses of new pots.
The study, published in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology in October, found that rice cooked in new pots contained up to 305 micrograms of lead per kilogram, while khichuri contained up to 420 micrograms. Both levels were substantially higher than the US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) limit of 10 micrograms per kilogram for food intended for babies and young children.
Researchers tested 7 used aluminium pots collected from households and 20 new pots purchased from a local supplier. Lead was detected in food cooked in every new pot and 6 of the 7 used pots.
The findings raise concerns about locally manufactured cookware, much of which is produced by melting scrap metal without adequate screening for contaminants.
Lead levels in food declined with repeated use of new pots but remained detectable during the third cooking. Researchers also found that scrubbing new pots with steel-wire sponges released about 5 times more lead than leaving them unscrubbed. Stirring food with metal spatulas also increased lead release.
Based on typical rice consumption among children in rural Bangladesh, researchers estimated that a child eating rice cooked in such a pot could ingest more than 5 times the FDA's reference level for daily lead intake from food. The estimate was based on a model rather than direct measurements of children's exposure.
“Lead can't be seen, smelled or tasted, so a pot that looks perfectly good can still be added to a family's food,” said Dr Jenna Forsyth, director of Project Unleaded at Stanford University's Human and Planetary Health program.
She said the study measured lead in both cookware and food to establish how everyday cooking pots could become a source of exposure.
Lead exposure can cause lasting damage to children's brain development, affecting learning and behavior. The World Health Organization (WHO) says there is no known safe level of lead in blood.
Dr Jesmin Sultana, assistant scientist at icddr,b's Environmental Health and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) program, said families should choose cookware with credible evidence of food safety, particularly when preparing meals for young children.
She advised households using locally made pots to avoid steel-wire scrubbers and cooking acidic dishes in them. However, she cautioned that these measures could not reliably make contaminated cookware safe.
The researchers said responsibility for preventing exposure should not rest solely on consumers, as lead contamination can occur during manufacturing. They called on the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority (BFSA) and the Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution (BSTI) to introduce and enforce clear safety requirements for cookware.
Proposed measures include screening scrap metal used in production, testing finished pots for lead release into food, and helping small-scale manufacturers access safer raw materials and testing facilities.
“Affordable cookware should also be safe cookware,” said Dr Md Mahbubur Rahman of icddr,b's Environmental Health and WASH program, urging authorities to establish and enforce standards for lead leaching from cookware.
The researchers acknowledged that the study was a small laboratory investigation and that further research is needed to assess other types of cookware and everyday cooking practices.
The study was supported by Stanford University's King Center on Global Development.

item.title: Proposal to cap Malaysia migration costs at Tk3 lakh
item.description:
Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury has sought proposals from recruiting agencies on fixing the cost of sending workers to Malaysia, with one agency owner suggesting a range of Tk2.5 lakh to Tk3 lakh.
The proposal was made at a meeting between the minister and representatives of recruiting agencies listed with Malaysia’s Foreign Workers Management System (FWMS) at the Bijoy 71 Hall of the Expatriates’ Welfare Building on Thursday afternoon.
During the meeting, agency owners raised various challenges they face in the recruitment process. Asked about the possible cost of sending workers to Malaysia, one agency owner said they could facilitate the process for Tk2.5 lakh to Tk3 lakh, while suggesting that the amount could be increased if necessary.
In response, Ariful Haque said the proposal could help restore public confidence by reducing the financial burden on aspiring migrant workers and their families.
“We have received a specific proposal of Tk2.5 lakh to Tk3 lakh. This will reassure people across the country that they will not have to sell their land or cattle to send their sons abroad. The government will also extend support accordingly,” he said.
The recruiting agency owners also urged the government to announce the resumption of medical examinations for workers to facilitate the speedy reopening of the Malaysian labour market.
State Minister for Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Nurul Haque urged recruiting agencies to keep their profit margins reasonable and refrain from making excessive profits.
“We understand that processing visas involves costs. You have to run offices and maintain staff, so making a profit is normal. However, it should be within a reasonable and acceptable limit, not excessive,” he said.
On determining migration costs for the Malaysian labour market, the state minister said the minister had sought the agencies’ opinions and several representatives had shared their proposals.
“We will hold an official meeting on the matter and then consider what the migration cost should be,” he added.

item.title: PM envisions modernized Mongla Port as economic hub for southwest, northwest regions
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday said the modernization and expansion of Mongla Port will turn it into a promising economic hub for the country’s south-western and north-western regions, with the government planning to expand road connectivity, port supply chains and cargo transport facilities from Pantagraph to the Bay of Bengal.
“If Mongla Port is modernized and its facilities are expanded...It will become a promising economic hub for the country’s south-west and north-west,” he said.
The prime minister said this while addressing the foundation stone laying ceremony of the Tk 4,068 crore “Mongla Port Facilities Expansion and Modernization Project” in Mongla on Thursday morning.
He said the capacity building and modernization of the port will strengthen trade links with different parts of the country and help expand economic activities.
There is huge scope to expand economic activities in the south-western region, including Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jessore, centered on the port, he said.
The prime minister said, “Development of Khan Jahan Ali Airport is also one of our priorities. In the present global order, it is extremely important to keep energy and food security effective above all.”
“I firmly believe Mongla Port, as a complementary port for importing fuel, fertilizer, foodgrains and industrial raw materials and exporting domestic products, can further enrich national economic security,” he added.
Tarique Rahman said the initiative will help strengthen the country’s industry, trade and economic security, and add sustainable socio-economic value, especially in youth employment, entrepreneurs’ confidence in investment and balanced regional development.
He laid the foundation stone of the project, which includes two container jetties and related infrastructure, at 11:15 am.
Once the project is implemented, container trains from Dhaka’s Kamalapur Inland Container Depot (ICD) will be able to run directly to Mongla Port, turning it into a major import-export hub of the country, he said.
Under the modernization project, necessary infrastructure, including a modern container terminal, yard and cargo handling facilities, is being built, he said.
“If the work is completed on time, the economic condition of this region will change, Inshallah, and a new door of economic possibilities will open not only for this region but for the whole country,” he added.
Noting that the project’s success does not end with the completion of construction, the Prime Minister said, “The real success of any project depends on how much port service quality improves, how much time and cost of cargo handling fall, how much investment and employment grow, and how much the environment is protected.”
“We must follow international environmental and safety standards, build climate-resilient infrastructure and increase the use of renewable energy,” he said.
In this connection, he stressed on eco-friendly service management, pollution control and safe waste management of ships.
He also said fire safety, trained manpower and emergency response capacity are needed to handle hazardous operations.
Highlighting the country’s economic target, the prime minister said his government has set the goal of turning Bangladesh into a $1 trillion economy by 2030.
“To achieve this goal, top priority is being given to investment, industrialization, export diversification, energy and food security, and skilled human resource development,” he said.
The prime minister urged international stakeholders, development partners and, in particular, expatriate Bangladeshis to come forward with investment to help make the country self-reliant.
In this context, he said the government is committed to ensuring a favorable investment climate, easy service procedures, reliable infrastructure and policy continuity.
“The modernization of Mongla Port is only one step in the plan to transform Bangladesh into a $1 trillion economy,” he added.
“So, it is extremely necessary to ensure the port’s navigability, the reliability of the navigation channel, the safe movement of ships and competitive port services,” he said.
The prime minister also said Mongla Port must now be made attractive to international shipping companies and developed into a first calling port on suitable commercial and operational terms.
He said the government has taken steps to supply gas as quickly as possible to existing industries and to those who may set up new ones in the area. “Work has already been started to this end,” he said.
Recalling the region’s industrial past, he said Khulna and the surrounding areas once had many mills and factories. “We want to bring back that lost heritage,” he said
Minister for Road Transport and Bridges, Railways and Shipping Shaikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Shipping and Bridges Md Razib Ahsan, State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shaikh Faridul Islam, Mongla Port Authority Chairman Rear Admiral Arif Ahmed Mostafa and CRCC Chairman Dai Hegen spoke on the occasion.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury and other senior officials were present.

item.title: PM: People will give conspirators befitting reply, as in 2024
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday said the people will unitedly give a befitting reply, as they did in 2024, to those conspiring to destroy the country’s industries.
In this context, he assured workers that a new minimum wage will be fixed for them within a month or two.
“We will stand against the conspirators with all our strength, together with the people of the country, the working people and our brothers and sisters among the workers. Just as the people of Bangladesh gave them a befitting reply in 2024, they will be given a befitting reply in the same way in the days ahead.,” he said.
The prime minister was addressing a roadside meeting at Katakhali intersection on the Khulna-Mongla highway at 12:30 pm, on his way to visit the mazar of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali (R) in Bagerhat.
Tarique Rahman said the people’s government has been established and has taken up work and plans to change the fate of the general masses, but the conspirators want to derail them.
“The people and the country’s workers must stand up against these conspiracies so that the conspirators get no opportunity in any way. Now is the time to build our country and change the fate of our people,” he said.
Warning the conspirators, the premier said, “We will give a befitting reply to these conspirators with all our strength, Inshallah. Our goal is one: ‘Let us work, build the country, Bangladesh first’ (Korbo Kaj, Gorbo Desh; Sobar Agee Bangladesh).”
Tarique Rahman said those who had failed to improve people's living conditions over the past 15-16 years, deprived them of their voting rights and siphoned off the country's wealth abroad were forced to flee following the mass uprising on August 5, 2024. “They (ousted forces) are now pulling strings from across the border and trying to create disorder and chaos in the country. Not only that, they are about to destroy the country’s mills and factories,” he said.
Tarique Rahman said the mills and factories are the wealth of the people and of the country’s workers. “If they are destroyed, the working people will be the first to suffer. My brothers and sisters among the workers will suffer the most, and their children’s future will be ruined,” he said.
On the wage board, the prime minister said the elected government is working day and night to solve the country’s problems and expand industry and trade so that people can live well. “We know the workers have made some demands about their wages. You have seen that we have already formed a wage board to consider those demands,” he said.
The wage board has already started work and will fix a new minimum wage within a month or two, he said, so that workers can live even better.
The prime minister said BNP had promised, if it formed the government, to create jobs, reopen closed public and private mills and factories, and encourage local and foreign investors to set up new industries.
“We will try to reopen the mills and factories that have been shut down across the country at different times, especially the public ones. Alongside that, we will encourage investors at home and abroad to set up new mills and factories, because we want to create employment for the country’s young people,” he said.
Recalling that Khulna was once one of the country’s leading industrial regions, he said many of its factories have closed over time for various reasons.
The government wants to set up thousands of factories, from the south-west, including Khulna, Bagerhat, Kushtia and Chuadanga, to Panchagarh in the north, added the premier.
Earlier in the morning, the prime minister attended the signing ceremony of an MoU on economic and infrastructure cooperation between Invest Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), a Chinese state-owned company, in Mongla, and later laid the foundation stone of the Mongla Port expansion and modernization project.
After the roadside meeting, he visited the mazar of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali (R) in Bagerhat and also attend the opening ceremony of Notun Kuri Sports (Season-2) at the Khulna District Stadium in the afternoon.

item.title: 20 crude bombs, 41 torch-sticks seized in Mirpur
item.description:
Police have recovered 20 crude bombs, 41 torch-sticks and around two litres of kerosene during an operation near the Ansar Camp in Paikpara, Mirpur.
The items were seized on Thursday following a tip-off, according to Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP).
Hasan Mohammad Naser Bikabdar, deputy commissioner of the DMP's Mirpur division, confirmed the recovery.
He said police received information overnight that suspected crude bombs and torch-sticks had been left on the road in front of the Ansar Camp.
A team led by Mirpur Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Hafizur Rahman recovered 20 crude bombs, including 15 inside three paper bags and five lying on the road.
Police also seized 41 torch-sticks, around two litres of kerosene in two bottles inside a shopping bag, and several sheets of soft polystyrene, commonly known as thermocol.
The 20 crude bombs were later detonated in two separate operations inside a pit dug at an open area of a construction site belonging to the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, near Hakkani Goli in Kalyanpur, the deputy commissioner said.
Legal proceedings are underway, he added.
Bikabdar also said the recovery took place around the time of the arrest of Al Mahmud Tarek, a former central organising secretary of the banned Chhatra League and former general secretary of its Dhaka College unit.
He said police suspected the seized materials might have been intended for a major act of sabotage.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,272 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours ending at 8:00am on Thursday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,272 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) classified the latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,167, while confirmed deaths have remained the same at 105.
A total of 1,327 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 235,475.
Meanwhile, 69 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, pushing laboratory-confirmed infections to 24,219.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 209,854 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 201,153 have recovered, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Two motorcyclists killed in collision with covered van on Airport Road
item.description:
Two men riding a motorcycle were killed after it collided with a covered van in front of Xinxian Restaurant on the capital's Airport Road on Thursday morning.
The deceased were identified as Arifur Rahman, 40, and Falu, 55. Both worked at scrap shops in Postogola.
The accident occurred around 10am. Falu died at the scene, while Arifur succumbed to his injuries at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).
Abul Hasan, a tea stall owner who helped take Arifur to the hospital, said a private car first collided head-on with a covered van in front of the restaurant. A motorcycle then crashed into the same covered van.
One of the motorcyclists died on the spot, while the other, identified as Arifur, was taken to DMCH by police in critical condition, he said.
Fazle Rabbi, a scrap dealer from Postogola, said Arifur worked at his shop, Mitu Enterprise, while Falu was employed at a neighbouring scrap shop.
The two were heading to Tongi in Gazipur to buy scrap materials when the accident occurred, Rabbi said, adding that he learned about the incident over the phone.
Arifur was the son of Awal Molla and hailed from Bedbaria village in Bera upazila of Pabna. He lived in Konapara, Demra, and is survived by two sons and a daughter.
Further details about Falu were not immediately available.
Airport Police Station Sub-Inspector Manik Mahmud confirmed that the motorcycle collided with a covered van in front of Xinjian Restaurant, leaving one person dead at the scene and another dead at the hospital.
The covered van's driver also sustained minor injuries. Police seized both the covered van and the motorcycle.

item.title: Sheikh Hasina's former information adviser arrested in murder case
item.description:
Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury, former information adviser to then prime minister Sheikh Hasina and former chairman of television channel DBC, has been arrested in connection with a murder case filed with Jatrabari police station over the anti-discrimination movement.
Md Shafiqul Islam, additional commissioner (Detective Branch) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), confirmed the arrest Wednesday night.
He said the case was filed on August 26, 2024.
Meanwhile, DBC News journalist Rajib Ghosh was released around midnight after prolonged questioning. He was handed over to his family at around 2am after signing a personal bond.
Earlier on Wednesday afternoon, Detective Branch (DB) officials took Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury and Rajib Ghosh into custody from the DBC News office in Mohakhali, Dhaka, and questioned them at the DB office.
Md Aktar Hossain, deputy commissioner of the DMP's Media and Public Relations Division, earlier said an “unwanted situation” had arisen at the DBC office over the broadcast of a news report.
He said the DB went to the office after receiving information about the incident, following which the two men were taken to the DB office.

item.title: Sagar-Runi murder case: Probe report postponed for 131st time
item.description:
A Dhaka court has postponed the submission of the investigation report in the journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi murder case until December 9, marking the 131st delay in the case.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam set the new date after a hearing on Thursday, as the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), the current investigating agency, failed to submit its report.
The information was confirmed by Rafiqul Islam, a sub-inspector of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s prosecution division.
Sagar, news editor of private television channel Maasranga TV, and Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were murdered at their rented home in West Rajabazar, Dhaka, on February 11, 2012. Their four-and-a-half-year-old son, Mahir Sarowar Megh, was at home at the time.
Runi’s brother, Nowsher Alam Roman, filed a murder case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar Police Station.
The accused are Rafiqul Islam, Bakul Mia, Masum Mintu, Kamrul Islam alias Arun, Abu Sayeed, the couple’s two residential security guards Palash Rudra Pal and Enayet Ahmed, and their friend Tanvir Rahman Khan. Tanvir and Palash are out on bail, while the others are in jail.
The case was initially investigated by Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police before being transferred to the Detective Branch of Dhaka Metropolitan Police and later to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB).
On September 30 last year, the High Court directed the formation of a high-powered task force comprising experienced investigators from different law enforcement agencies to investigate the murders. A High Court bench comprising Justices Farah Mahbub and Muhammad Mahbub Ul Islam ordered that the task force be formed through the Ministry of Home Affairs.
On October 23, 2025, the government formed a four-member task force in line with the court directive, with the PBI chief as its convener.

item.title: Workers take to streets again in Ashulia, more than 100 factories shut
item.description:
Labour unrest flared up again in the Ashulia industrial zone on Thursday as garment workers left their factories to press for higher wages, prompting more than 100 factories to suspend operations and disrupting traffic on the Abdullahpur-Baipail road.
Workers initially reported for duty at around 8am, registering their attendance by punching their ID cards. They later left their workplaces, gathered outside other factories and urged workers inside to join the protests.
As the unrest spread, more than 100 factories declared general holidays, and workers took to the streets.
The protesters occupied the Abdullahpur-Baipail road, disrupting traffic. Police intervened at several points to disperse them, after which groups of workers moved to nearby side roads.
Meanwhile, the situation in the Savar industrial zone remained relatively calm on Thursday morning, a day after workers blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway and set fire to a police van and a motorcycle.
Workers said the Wage Board Commission had announced that a wage increase would take effect in December, but the amount had not been disclosed. They said the uncertainty had contributed to the continuation of their protests.
Security was tightened across the industrial zone to prevent further unrest. Police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel were deployed, while police armoured vehicles were stationed at key points.
Industrial Police-1 Superintendent Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said the overall situation in the Ashulia area under his unit's jurisdiction was stable.
He said 70 of the 1,863 factories under the unit's jurisdiction had suspended operations for the day, while the rest remained open.
According to Mominul, some people began throwing bricks and stones in the Jamgara area after workers from several factories were dismissed. When police detained some of them, others attacked officers and vandalised police vehicles.
Police then used sound grenades and tear gas to bring the situation under control, he said.
He added that around 2,500 workers had recently held a peaceful march from Jirabo to Envoy factory to protest the killing of a worker in Gazipur.
Mominul said Industrial Police did not have a confirmed figure for those detained in connection with Thursday's incidents and that no one was in their custody at the time of his statement.
He said five BGB platoons, equipped with armoured personnel carriers, had been deployed in the area.
Local police and Industrial Police were coordinating their operations, and legal action was being taken where necessary, he added.
Mominul said most workers wanted to return to their jobs but alleged that outsiders were provoking them and disrupting factory operations, including through social media.
He said the government had formed a Minimum Wage Board and that the new wage structure was scheduled to take effect from January. He added that factory owners were committed to implementing the new minimum wage and that law enforcement agencies were urging workers to return to work.
The police official also said authorities were trying to identify people allegedly inciting unrest through social media. He claimed several people had been detained and information had been obtained during questioning, but declined to disclose their identities, citing the ongoing investigation.
He further alleged that outsiders were using workers as a front to create unrest and sharing information on social media about protest locations and incidents of vandalism. He said it was not clear whether the individuals had any political backing.

item.title: Gazipur garment workers return to factories peacefully
item.description:
Garment workers across Gazipur's industrial zones returned to their workplaces peacefully on Thursday morning, following several days of unrest over wage demands and the blacklisting of workers.
Workers reported for duty in Shafipur, Chandra and Palli Bidyut areas of Kaliakair upazila, as well as Bhogra Bypass, Konabari, Kashimpur and Salna in Gazipur metropolitan area.
To maintain law and order, 25 platoons of security personnel remain deployed across the industrial zones, supported by 25 executive magistrates.
The deployment includes 12 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), eight of the Special Reserve Battalion (SRB) and five of Ansar, Arif Hossain, assistant commissioner (Media) at the Gazipur deputy commissioner's office, said.
According to Industrial Police and local sources, workers began arriving at factories in the morning, some using factory-provided transport and others travelling on foot. Workers were seen entering factories in an orderly manner, with no reports of fresh unrest.
Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said workers had joined their shifts peacefully.
He said police and other security forces had intensified patrols to prevent any untoward incidents and maintain law and order.
The situation remained calm and stable amid the deployment of joint security forces, he added.
In recent days, protests and clashes broke out in several industrial areas of Gazipur as workers demanded a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, reinstatement of laid-off workers and an end to the blacklisting of workers who took part in the demonstrations.

item.title: Police on high alert in Mirpur amid garment workers' protests
item.description:
Law enforcement agencies remain on high alert in Mirpur-11 following protests by garment workers demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
Additional police personnel have been deployed in the area, with officers patrolling roads and preventing gatherings on streets and sidewalks.
The heightened security measures have been in place since Thursday morning.
Pallabi Police Station Officer-in-Charge Jalal Uddin said the workers had not taken to the streets on Thursday, but police remained prepared to respond to any situation.
“The workers have not taken to the streets today; however, we remain on alert. Additional police have been deployed, and patrols are being conducted. The situation remains normal,” he said.
On November 1, garment workers blocked roads in Mirpur to press their demand for a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. Clashes and chases between workers and police continued intermittently from morning until afternoon.
At one point, a police vehicle was set on fire beneath the Mirpur-11 metro rail station. Police later detained several people from different parts of Mirpur in connection with the incident.
Workers also staged protests in Mirpur on Monday and Tuesday.
Similar demonstrations over the wage demand have taken place in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj, triggering clashes, disrupting production and forcing many factories to suspend operations.
Meanwhile, Taufiq Sheikh, a garment worker injured during the unrest in Gazipur, died at Shin-Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara, Dhaka, on Tuesday while undergoing treatment.

item.title: Two auto-rickshaw drivers killed after truck hits vehicles in Dhaka
item.description:
Two auto-rickshaw drivers were killed and another person injured after a truck lost control, hit two auto-rickshaws and mounted a sidewalk in Postogola, Kadamtali, in the capital early Thursday.
The deceased were identified as Md Jahangir Poddar, 40, and Md Zakir Hossain, 50.
The accident occurred around 3am. The victims were taken to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), where doctors declared Jahangir dead at 4:25am. Zakir was admitted for treatment but later died. The third injured person is receiving medical care.
Both men were auto-rickshaw drivers who had been waiting for passengers at the time of the accident.
Sub-Inspector Md Jamal Hossain of Kadamtali police station said the truck had been seized, but its driver fled the scene.
“The bodies of the two victims have been sent to the Dhaka Medical College morgue for autopsies. Efforts are underway to apprehend the driver,” he said.
Hridoy, a colleague of Jahangir, said three people were injured in the accident. Two died, while the third received treatment at the hospital.
Zakir was the son of Jinnat Ali of Ajmiriganj upazila in Habiganj. He lived in the Pakar Matha area of Mohammadbagh, Kadamtali.
Jahangir was the son of Shah Alam Poddar of Patuakhali Sadar upazila. He lived in the Nama Shyampur area.

item.title: AB Bank disburses agricultural loans in Sirajganj
item.description:
AB Bank PLC has disbursed agricultural loans to marginal farmers in Sadar Upazila, Sirajganj.
The loans were disbursed among the farmers at a program held at Sirajganj Upazila Parisad Auditorium with a view to developing the agricultural sector and strengthening food security.
Iftekhar Enam Awal, deputy managing director, AB Bank, presided over the program while ZM Babar Khan, additional managing director attended the program as chief guest.
Md Mamun Khan, Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sirajganj Sadar, Joynal Abedin, additional director, Agricultural Credit Department-2, Head Office, Bangladesh Bank, Shantanu Biswas, joint director, Agricultural Credit Department-1, Head Office, Bangladesh Bank, and SM Nasim Hossain, Upazila agriculture officer, were present as special guests.
Senior officials of the bank and local dignitaries were also present at the event.

item.title: Chinese students perform dragon, lion dances at Notun Kuri Sports opening
item.description:
Traditional Chinese dragon and lion dances performed by a group of students from China added a cultural touch to the opening ceremony of Notun Kuri Sports (Season 2) in Khulna on Thursday.
The students from Yunnan Minzu University in Kunming, Yunnan Province, China, performed the dances in the presence of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at Khulna District Stadium, said Prime Minister’s Assistant Press Secretary, Abdullah Al Mahmud Shahriar.
The performance was part of sports and cultural diplomacy between Bangladesh and China.
Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Protishtan (BKSP) and Yunnan Minzu University have an ongoing sports training exchange program.
Under the program, BKSP coaches provide cricket training to students of the Chinese university, while its coaches train BKSP students in wushu, a traditional Chinese martial art.
BKSP athletes also receive training from Chinese coaches in table tennis, athletics, badminton, swimming and diving.
The training exchange and cultural performances reflect the growing sports and cultural cooperation between the two countries.
Earlier, the prime minister inaugurated the “Notun Kuri Sports” (Season-2) at Khulna District Stadium by releasing balloons and pigeons.
State Minister for Youth and Sports Md Aminul Haque and Whip and Khulna-3 MP Rakibul Islam were present.

item.title: Indian visa applicants face new form requirement
item.description:
The Indian High Commission in Dhaka has made it mandatory for all visa applicants to submit a prescribed ‘Visa Undertaking Form’ along with their applications.
The high commission announced the requirement in an urgent advisory published on its visa portal on Thursday.
Under the new instructions, applicants must download the designated form from the link provided by the high commission, fill it out correctly, scan it and upload it with their online applications through the NIC Visa Application Portal. Applications submitted using any other format will not be accepted.
The high commission said the initiative aims to make the visa application process more transparent and orderly.
The one-page form requires applicants to declare that they will visit India only for the purpose stated in their applications, that they reside within the jurisdiction of the Indian High Commission in Dhaka on the date of application, and that all information provided is accurate.
In the personal details section, applicants must provide five mandatory details: their name as shown in the passport, passport number, nationality, date of birth and current address in Dhaka.
They must also clearly state the purpose of their visit, such as tourism, business, medical treatment or attending a conference.
The undertaking includes commitments to return to their home country immediately after the visit, not overstay their visa and comply with Indian laws, regulations and culture while in the country.
The form warns that violations of Indian laws may lead to visa cancellation and affect an applicant’s eligibility for future visas.
Applicants must sign the form and mention the place and date of signing. For minors, both parents are required to sign it.

PM Tarique’s Khulna visit brings big promises for industry, jobs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday unveiled plans to develop an industrial corridor stretching from Mongla in the southwest to Panchagarh in the north, seeking to revive struggling industrial regions, attract investment and create employment through expanded port facilities, energy infrastructure and improved connectivity.
During a daylong visit to Bagerhat and Khulna, he laid the foundation stone of a Tk4,068 crore project to expand and modernise Mongla Port, witnessed the signing of an investment cooperation agreement with a Chinese state-owned company and pledged to reopen closed factories while encouraging the establishment of new industries.
The prime minister also assured workers that a new minimum wage would be fixed within one or two months, as garment workers continued demonstrations across several industrial areas demanding higher pay.
Addressing a roadside meeting at Katakhali intersection on the Khulna-Mongla highway, Tarique said his government wanted to restore Khulna’s former industrial prominence and extend industrial development across Bagerhat, Kushtia, Chuadanga and other districts towards Panchagarh.
He said the government would gradually develop the necessary electricity, gas and transport infrastructure to attract factories and generate employment along the proposed corridor.
Earlier, the prime minister laid the foundation stone of the Tk4,068 crore Mongla Port expansion and modernisation project, which includes two container jetties and supporting infrastructure to increase cargo-handling capacity and improve services.
Speaking at the ceremony, he described Mongla as a potential economic hub for the country’s southwestern and northwestern regions.
He said modernising the port would help expand trade and industrial activities in Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jashore while strengthening economic connectivity with northern districts.
The government also plans to improve road links between Panchagarh and Mongla, expand port supply chains and facilitate cargo transportation.
According to the prime minister’s deputy press secretary, the project would enable direct container train services between Kamalapur Inland Container Depot in Dhaka and Mongla Port once the necessary facilities are operational.
Tarique also identified the development and operation of Khan Jahan Ali Airport as a government priority.
He stressed that the project’s success would depend not merely on completing infrastructure but also on reducing cargo-handling costs, improving efficiency and attracting investment.
At Mongla Port, the prime minister witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Invest Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) on economic and infrastructure cooperation.
Invest Bangladesh Member (Industrial Zones) Saleh Ahmed and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation Chairman Li Chongyang signed the agreement.
The cooperation framework covers potential investment in energy, industrial and environmentally sustainable infrastructure, transport, logistics and human resource development.
Tarique later held discussions with a Chinese delegation led by CRCC Chairman Dai Hegen.
He urged Chinese investors to establish industries around Mongla and emphasised the importance of reliable electricity and gas supplies for industrial expansion.
The prime minister also thanked the Chinese delegation for supporting opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to secure employment with Chinese companies in the Middle East.
The prime minister said the government wanted to reopen closed mills and factories, including state-owned establishments, and encourage domestic and foreign investment to create employment.
Later, he visited the shrine of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali in Bagerhat, where he offered prayers.
In Khulna, he inaugurated the second season of Notun Kuri Sports at the district stadium, highlighting the importance of sports, arts and cultural activities alongside academic education.
He said the government was committed to fulfilling its election promises and developing the next generation through education and extracurricular activities.
Around 1.6 million children are participating in the nationwide sporting initiative, according to the program details provided.
The prime minister also reiterated that his government would continue efforts to strengthen the economy despite global challenges.

item.title: Historic leadership firsts for minorities across US in midterm vote
item.description:
The US midterm vote ushered in a wave of historic leadership firsts across the country on Tuesday, electoral milestones on a night that saw voters issue a sharp rejection of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator, the first Muslim senator and the first female Native American governor all won groundbreaking elections in the vote that racked up resounding gains for Democrats.
Bill Shiebler -- chief strategy officer at the non-profit State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity -- told AFP the night was “a huge rebuke against hate and division.”
“We’re witnessing an electorate that increasingly sees itself in its leaders, and the leaders who come out of communities they now represent,” Shiebler said.
In Michigan, leftist Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The former medical administrator drew huge campaign crowds but faced a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric from his detractors in the bruising race.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations advocacy group praised El-Sayed for persevering despite “endless Islamophobic attacks.”
“Our communities worked hard to make sure our voices were heard and that we are properly represented in the Senate,” the organization said.
“This is what is possible when we show up and vote together.”
In the southern state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the race for governor, making her the first Black woman elected to the top office in any US state.
A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, a win that returns the governor’s office to Democrats after more than two decades of Republican control.
Democratic Representative Chris Pappas, meanwhile, will become the first openly gay man to serve in the US Senate after winning in New Hampshire. He has served in the US House of Representatives since 2019.
“No one should be discriminated against because of who they are or who they love,” he said on his website.
In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor, beating Republican Gregg Hull.
A member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe, she had served as the secretary of the interior under former president Joe Biden, the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary.
Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota was elected as the first female Native American senator.
The sweeping midterm rebuke of Trump also saw a number of state-level electoral firsts, including the first Latina governor in Texas with Gina Hinojosa’s victory.
Looking ahead, if the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins the speakership as expected in the new Congress, he would become the first Black speaker of the House in US history.
“This was a historic election where people decided to believe in themselves and really lean into the hope about the promise of this country, rebuking an effort to snuff out people’s voices,” Shiebler said.

item.title: Health minister: Five Dhaka hospitals to launch PPP-based healthcare services
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Thursday said the government plans to launch improved healthcare services under a public-private partnership (PPP) model, initially at five hospitals in Dhaka on a trial basis.
“Plans are underway to expand the healthcare program to other cities,” he said while addressing an event held at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College Hospital (SZMCH) in Bogra.
The health minister said discussions with the five hospitals had been finalised, but another meeting would be held next week to determine the fees private partners would charge. The pilot program would begin once financial arrangements were settled, he added.
"We will initially introduce the program on a trial basis at five hospitals in Dhaka before expanding it to other cities. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is interested in the initiative, and we are working to implement it," he said.
Describing SZMCH as a major healthcare centre for northern Bangladesh, the minister said the government was considering expanding access to advanced treatment for complex diseases, including cancer and liver conditions.
Hospital authorities had been asked to submit written lists of their problems, which would be addressed gradually, he added.
On the shortage of doctors and the absence of a separate paediatric ICU at SZMCH, the minister said the government planned to establish around 20 new ICUs across the country, including one in Bogra. He said 17 of the 500 newly appointed doctors had been posted to different healthcare facilities in Bogra, with more appointments planned.
Recruitment of another 5,000 doctors is also underway. Applications have closed, and the Public Service Commission is conducting the interview process, he added.
Blaming corruption and mismanagement over the past 17 years for the deterioration of the healthcare sector, he said the current government was working to restore discipline and improve services.

item.title: QS Asia Rankings: DU retains top position from Bangladesh, 16th in South Asia
item.description:
Dhaka University has retained its position as the top university in Bangladesh in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, securing 136th place among Asian universities and 16th among those in South Asia.
The UK-based international higher education and research organization Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) published the rankings on November 3. DU also held the top position among Bangladeshi universities in last year's rankings.
According to a press release issued by DU, a total of 1,722 universities from 26 countries across Asia have been included in this year's rankings. The University of Hong Kong secured the first position, followed by Peking University of China.
The QS Asia University Rankings assess universities based on several indicators, including academic reputation, faculty-student ratio, research quality and impact, the proportion of staff holding PhD degrees, international research collaboration, and the number of international faculty members and students.
DU Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr ABM Obaidul Islam expressed his satisfaction over the university's position in the international rankings. "This position in the international rankings is a matter of joy and pride for us. Consistently retaining the top position among Bangladeshi universities is recognition of collective efforts of our teachers, students, researchers and all concerned," he said.
However, he said the university's goal was not merely to maintain its ranking but to further strengthen its position internationally through improvement in the quality of education and research.
The vice-chancellor said enriching the academic and research environment, expanding research facilities, strengthening international collaborations and creating opportunities for students to develop globally competitive skills were among the university's key priorities.
